source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 6 (PDF 119-138, printed 116-135); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 6 (Heat and Thermodynamics), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.
6.1 Assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases

blocks.prompt: 1 Thermodynamics is the branch of physics that deals with:

options.text: motion of charges in a circuit
the structure of the atomic nucleus
relationships and conversions between heat and other forms of energy

blocks.explanation: Thermodynamics deals with the relationships and conversions between heat and other forms of energy (6.1).

book_ref.quote: deals with the relationships and conversions between heat and other forms of energy

blocks.prompt: 2 Thermodynamics plays a key role in technology because almost all the raw energy available for our use is liberated as:
blocks.explanation: Almost all the raw energy available for our use is liberated in the form of heat (6.1).

book_ref.quote: almost all the raw energy available for our use is liberated in the form of heat

blocks.prompt: 3 The kinetic theory of gases explains the behaviour of gases on the basis of:

options.text: the motion of their constituent particles
the shape of the container only
the chemical bonds inside each molecule

blocks.explanation: The kinetic theory explains the behaviour of gases based on the motion of their constituent particles (6.1).

book_ref.quote: explains the behaviour of gases based on the motion of their constituent particles

blocks.prompt: 4 According to the kinetic theory, between collisions gas molecules move:
blocks.explanation: Gas molecules are in perpetual random motion and move in straight lines until they collide with a molecule or a wall (6.1).

book_ref.quote: They move in straight lines until they collide

blocks.prompt: 5 In the kinetic theory, gas particles are treated as point masses because:

options.text: their volume is negligible compared to the total volume of the gas
they never collide with each other

blocks.explanation: The volume of individual molecules is negligible compared to the total volume of the gas, so they are point masses (6.1).

book_ref.quote: the particles are considered point masses with no significant volume

blocks.prompt: 6 According to the kinetic theory, ideal gas molecules exert forces on each other:

options.text: only when they are far apart

blocks.explanation: There are no attractive or repulsive forces between molecules except during collisions (6.1).

book_ref.quote: The particles do not exert any force on each other except during collisions

blocks.prompt: 7 Collisions of gas molecules with each other and with the walls are perfectly elastic. This means:

options.text: all kinetic energy changes into heat
there is no net loss of kinetic energy

blocks.explanation: In perfectly elastic collisions there is no net loss of kinetic energy; total kinetic energy is conserved (6.1).

book_ref.quote: there is no net loss of kinetic energy during collisions

blocks.prompt: 8 The very large number of particles in a gas allows us to describe its properties using:

options.text: the motion of one chosen molecule

blocks.explanation: A gas contains a large number of particles, which allows statistical methods to describe its properties (6.1).

book_ref.quote: This large number allows for the use of statistical methods

blocks.prompt: 9 The average kinetic energy of gas particles is directly proportional to the:
blocks.explanation: Assumption 6: average kinetic energy is directly proportional to the absolute (kelvin) temperature (6.1).

book_ref.quote: directly proportional to the absolute temperature of the gas

blocks.prompt: 10 When the temperature of a gas is increased, the speed of its particles:
blocks.explanation: As temperature increases, the average kinetic energy and hence the speed of the particles increases (6.1).

book_ref.quote: as the temperature increases, the speed of the gas particles also increases

blocks.prompt: 11 The pressure exerted by a gas on the walls of its container is due to:

options.text: collisions of gas particles with the walls

blocks.explanation: Pressure is due to the collisions of gas particles with the walls; the force during collisions generates pressure (6.1).

book_ref.quote: is due to the collisions of gas particles with the walls

blocks.prompt: 12 In the kinetic theory, the time taken for a collision is:

options.text: longer than the time between collisions
equal to the time between collisions
extremely short compared to the time between collisions

blocks.explanation: Collision time is extremely short compared to the time between collisions, which simplifies the analysis (6.1).

book_ref.quote: extremely short compared to the time between collisions

blocks.prompt: 13 Real gases deviate most from the assumptions of the kinetic theory at:

options.text: low pressure and low temperature only in vacuum
any pressure at very high temperature

blocks.explanation: Real gases deviate due to intermolecular forces and finite molecular volume, especially at high pressures and low temperatures (6.1).

book_ref.quote: especially at high pressures and low temperatures

blocks.prompt: 14 Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour because of:

options.text: intermolecular forces and finite molecular volume

blocks.explanation: The deviations are due to intermolecular forces and finite molecular volume (6.1).

book_ref.quote: real gases exhibit deviations due to intermolecular forces and finite molecular volume

blocks.prompt: 15 A gas that obeys the kinetic theory of gases is called:
blocks.explanation: A gas that obeys the kinetic theory of gases is termed an ideal gas (6.1).

book_ref.quote: A gas that obeys kinetic theory of gases is termed as an ideal gas

blocks.prompt: 16 The value of the universal gas constant R used in the chapter is:
blocks.explanation: R = 8.3145 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (6.1); 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ is k_B and 6.02 × 10²³ is Nₐ.

book_ref.quote: R is universal gas constant (R = 8.3145 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)

blocks.prompt: 17 For a fixed amount of an ideal gas, PV = nRT shows that the product PV is directly proportional to:
blocks.explanation: Equation (6.1) implies that PV is directly proportional to the temperature (6.1).

book_ref.quote: product of pressure and volume is directly proportional to the temperature

blocks.prompt: 18 Two moles of an ideal gas at 300 K occupy 0.050 m³. Using R = 8.3145 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, its pressure is about:

book_ref.quote: Here P represents pressure, V is volume, n is number of moles

blocks.prompt: 19 The Boltzmann constant k_B is defined as:
blocks.explanation: The term R/Nₐ is the Boltzmann constant: k_B = R/Nₐ (Eq. 6.2).

book_ref.quote: The term R/Nₐ is termed as Boltzmann constant k_B.

blocks.prompt: 20 The value of the Boltzmann constant is:

book_ref.quote: Substituting the values of R and Nₐ, we have

blocks.prompt: 21 In terms of the Boltzmann constant, the ideal gas equation is:
blocks.explanation: Substituting k_B = R/Nₐ in PV = (N/Nₐ)RT gives PV = N k_B T (Eq. 6.3), where N is the number of molecules.

book_ref.quote: Equation (6.3) gives ideal gas equation in terms of Boltzmann constant.

blocks.prompt: 22 A sample of gas contains 1.204 × 10²⁴ molecules. Taking Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³, the number of moles is:

book_ref.quote: It can be defined as the number of atoms are molecules per unit Avogadro's number

blocks.prompt: 23 A gas at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and 300 K occupies 1.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Using k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹, the number of molecules is about:

book_ref.quote: Substituting Eq. (6.2) in Eq. (iii),

blocks.prompt: 24 Real gases approach ideal behaviour under:
blocks.explanation: Real gases approach ideal behaviour at low pressure and high temperature (6.1).

book_ref.quote: Real gases approach ideal behaviour under: (i) low pressure (ii) high temperature

blocks.prompt: 25 For a real gas behaving like an ideal gas, the energy of its molecules is:

options.text: only kinetic; potential energy is negligible
only potential; kinetic energy is negligible

blocks.explanation: When intermolecular forces are negligible, the P.E. of the molecules is negligible and they have only K.E. (6.1).

book_ref.quote: P.E. of the gas molecules is negligible and this have only K.E.

blocks.prompt: 26 The density of an ideal gas of molar mass M at pressure P and temperature T is given by:
blocks.explanation: With n = m/M, PV = (m/M)RT gives PM = (m/V)RT, so ρ = PM/RT (6.1).

book_ref.quote: In Eq. (6.1) n represents number of moles which can be given by

blocks.prompt: 27 At low pressure and high temperature, the density of a gas is:

options.text: high, so molecules are close together
low, so molecules are far apart

blocks.explanation: Since ρ ∝ P/T, density is low at low pressure and high temperature; molecules are far apart and forces become negligible (6.1).

book_ref.quote: The density of a gas will be low at low pressure and high temperature

blocks.prompt: 28 Oxygen (M = 0.032 kg mol⁻¹) is at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and 300 K. Treating it as an ideal gas (R = 8.3145 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹), its density is about:

book_ref.quote: So, the real gas behaves like an ideal gas at low pressure and high temperature.

blocks.prompt: 29 If the pressure of an ideal gas is kept constant and its kelvin temperature is doubled, its density becomes:
blocks.explanation: ρ ∝ P/T; at constant P, doubling T halves the density (6.1).

book_ref.quote: the intermolecular forces will be negligible

blocks.prompt: 30 The laws relating pressure, volume and temperature of an ideal gas, with one variable kept constant, are called:
blocks.explanation: The laws that relate P, V and T mutually for an ideal gas are termed gas laws (6.1).

book_ref.quote: The laws that relate these variables mutually for an ideal gas are termed as gas laws.

blocks.prompt: 31 Boyle's law relates the pressure and volume of a fixed mass of gas at constant:
blocks.explanation: Boyle's law gives the relation between P and V of a gas at constant temperature (6.1).

book_ref.quote: provides a relationship between pressure and volume of a gas at constant temperature

blocks.prompt: 32 Boyle's law was introduced by Robert Boyle in the year:
blocks.explanation: Robert Boyle introduced the law in 1662 (6.1). 1824 is Carnot's ideal engine and 1856 Clausius's entropy.

book_ref.quote: This law was introduced by Robert Boyle in 1662

blocks.prompt: 33 A fixed mass of gas occupies 9.0 L at 2.0 atm. At constant temperature its pressure is raised to 3.0 atm. Its new volume is:
blocks.explanation: Boyle's law: V₂ = P₁V₁/P₂ = 2.0 × 9.0/3.0 = 6.0 L (6.1).

book_ref.quote: pressure P exerted by a gas varies inversely with volume V

blocks.prompt: 34 A gas at 100 kPa is compressed at constant temperature from 4.0 L to 2.5 L. Its pressure becomes:

book_ref.quote: It is sated that for a fixed mass of an ideal gas

blocks.prompt: 35 At constant temperature, a graph of pressure P against volume V for a fixed mass of gas is:

options.text: a curve showing P decreasing as V increases
a straight line through the origin with positive slope

blocks.explanation: Boyle's law: P ∝ 1/V, so P falls as V rises along a curve (Fig. 6.1).

book_ref.quote: Boyle's law is shown graphically in Fig. 6.1.

blocks.prompt: 36 Charles' law relates the volume and temperature of a fixed mass of gas at constant:
blocks.explanation: Charles' law relates V and T of an ideal gas for a fixed mass at constant pressure (6.1).

book_ref.quote: Charles' law relates volume and temperature of an ideal gas for a fixed mass at constant pressure.

blocks.prompt: 37 Jacques Charles found the law that bears his name in about:
blocks.explanation: The book's 'Book correction' gives about 1787 (Gay-Lussac published it in 1802); the printed 1870 is a misprint (6.1).

book_ref.quote: Jacques Charles (1746–1823) found this law in about 1787

blocks.prompt: 38 A gas occupies 300 mL at 27 °C. At constant pressure it is heated to 127 °C. Its new volume is:
blocks.explanation: T₁ = 300 K, T₂ = 400 K; V₂ = V₁T₂/T₁ = 300 × 400/300 = 400 mL. Kelvin temperatures must be used (6.1).

book_ref.quote: the volume of given mass of gas at constant pressure is directly proportional to the absolute temperature

blocks.prompt: 39 A graph of volume V against absolute temperature T for a gas at constant pressure is:

options.text: a straight line through the origin

blocks.explanation: V ∝ T at constant pressure, so the V-T graph is a straight line through the origin (Fig. 6.2).

book_ref.quote: Graphically, it can be shown in Fig. 6.2.

blocks.prompt: 40 Gay-Lussac's law states that, at constant volume, the pressure of a fixed mass of gas varies:

options.text: inversely with the number of molecules

blocks.explanation: Gay-Lussac's law: P ∝ T at constant volume (6.1).

book_ref.quote: the pressure exerted by a gas varies directly with absolute temperature of the gas at constant volume

blocks.prompt: 41 A gas in a closed rigid container is at 150 kPa and 300 K. If it is heated to 400 K, its pressure becomes:
blocks.explanation: P₂ = P₁T₂/T₁ = 150 × 400/300 = 200 kPa (Gay-Lussac's law, 6.1).

book_ref.quote: Graphically, Gay-Lussac's law is shown in Fig. 6.3.

blocks.prompt: 42 Two bodies in thermal contact are in thermal equilibrium when they have the same:
blocks.explanation: At the same temperature there is no driving force for heat transfer, so the bodies remain in thermal equilibrium (6.1).

book_ref.quote: there is no driving force for heat transfer between them

blocks.prompt: 43 A metal spoon is put into hot coffee. When thermal equilibrium is reached:

options.text: heat keeps flowing from coffee to spoon
the spoon becomes hotter than the coffee
there is no net heat flow between them
heat flows from spoon to coffee

blocks.explanation: Eventually coffee and spoon reach the same temperature; there is then no net heat flow (6.1).

book_ref.quote: there is no net heat flow between the coffee and the spoon

blocks.prompt: 44 The internal energy of a substance is the sum of:

options.text: only the gravitational P.E. of the body
only the K.E. of the body as a whole
the heat supplied and the work done
all molecular kinetic and potential energies

blocks.explanation: Internal energy is the sum of all forms of molecular energies, kinetic and potential (6.2).

book_ref.quote: The sum of all forms of molecular energies (kinetic and potential) of a substance

blocks.prompt: 45 The internal energy of an ideal gas is generally the:
blocks.explanation: Ideal gas molecules are mass points exerting no forces, so internal energy is the translational K.E. of the molecules (6.2).

book_ref.quote: the internal energy of an ideal gas system is generally the translational K.E. of its molecules

blocks.prompt: 46 For an ideal gas system, internal energy is:

options.text: proportional to the square of its volume

blocks.explanation: For an ideal gas, internal energy is directly proportional to its temperature (6.2).

book_ref.quote: the internal energy is directly proportional to its temperature

blocks.prompt: 47 Besides translational and rotational energy, a diatomic gas molecule also has:

options.text: vibrational energy of the spring-like bond

blocks.explanation: A diatomic molecule also has vibrational energy associated with the spring-like bond between its atoms (6.2, Do You Know).

book_ref.quote: It also has vibrational energy associated with the spring like bond between its atoms.

blocks.prompt: 48 According to the kinetic theory, the average kinetic energy of a gas molecule at absolute temperature T is:

book_ref.quote: According to the kinetic theory of gases, the average kinetic energy of gas molecules is given by

blocks.prompt: 49 Using k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹, the average kinetic energy of a gas molecule at 400 K is:

book_ref.quote: where k_B is Boltzmann constant.

blocks.prompt: 50 The kelvin temperature of an ideal gas is raised from 300 K to 600 K. The average kinetic energy of its molecules becomes:
blocks.explanation: Average K.E. = (3/2) k_B T ∝ T; doubling T doubles the average K.E. (6.2).

book_ref.quote: the rise in temperature of an object reflects an increase in the internal kinetic energy

blocks.prompt: 51 During a phase change such as melting, the heat supplied:

options.text: changes the state of matter without changing temperature

blocks.explanation: In phase changes heat energy changes the state of matter without changing temperature (6.2, Tidbits).

book_ref.quote: phase changes (where heat energy changes the state of matter without changing temperature)

blocks.prompt: 52 Internal energy is a function of state. This means it:

options.text: depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path

blocks.explanation: Being a function of state, internal energy does not depend on path but on initial and final states; only its change matters (6.2).

book_ref.quote: Internal energy is a function of state.

blocks.prompt: 53 Internal energy is similar to gravitational potential energy in that:

options.text: only its change, not its absolute value, is important

blocks.explanation: Like P.E., it is the change in internal energy and not its absolute value which is important (6.2).

book_ref.quote: Thus, internal energy is similar to the gravitational P.E.

blocks.prompt: 54 According to the sign convention of the chapter, work done by the system on its environment is taken as:
blocks.explanation: Heat in and work out are positive: work done by the system is positive, work done on it is negative (6.3).

book_ref.quote: work done by the system on its environment is considered positive

blocks.prompt: 55 When the surroundings compress a gas, the work W in the first law is:
blocks.explanation: Work done on the system by the environment is taken as negative (6.3).

book_ref.quote: work done on the system by the environment is taken as negative

blocks.prompt: 56 Heat in and work out were defined as positive because the idea was first applied to the:
blocks.explanation: In the steam engine it was natural to transfer heat in and get work out, so both were taken positive (6.3).

book_ref.quote: The idea was first applied to the steam engine

blocks.prompt: 57 A gas at pressure P pushes a frictionless piston of area A. The force on the piston is:
blocks.explanation: The force exerted by the gas on the piston is F = PA (6.3).

book_ref.quote: The force F exerted by the gas on the piston is PA.

blocks.prompt: 58 In deriving W = PΔV, the gas is assumed to expand very slowly so that it:
blocks.explanation: The gas expands through ΔV very slowly so that it remains in equilibrium (6.3).

book_ref.quote: We assume that the gas expands through ΔV very slowly

blocks.prompt: 59 A gas expands against a constant pressure of 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa and its volume increases by 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³. The work done by the gas is:

book_ref.quote: the work W done by the gas is:

blocks.prompt: 60 Gas at 5000 N m⁻² pushes a piston of area 0.20 m² up through 5.0 cm at constant pressure. The work done by the gas is:

book_ref.quote: As the piston moves up through a small distance Δy

blocks.prompt: 61 On a P-V graph, the work done by a gas is equal to the:
blocks.explanation: The work done can be calculated as the area under the P-V graph (Fig. 6.5).

book_ref.quote: The work done can also be calculated by area of the curve under P-V graph

blocks.prompt: 62 The general principles dealing with heat energy and its transformation into mechanical energy are called:
blocks.explanation: These principles are known as the laws of thermodynamics (6.3).

book_ref.quote: These principles are known as laws of thermodynamics.

blocks.prompt: 63 The first law of thermodynamics is written as:
blocks.explanation: Q = ΔU + W (Eq. 6.5), with W the work done by the system.

book_ref.quote: the heat Q required will be the heat necessary to change the internal energy

blocks.prompt: 64 The underlying principle of the first law of thermodynamics is:
blocks.explanation: The first law expresses conservation of energy (6.4).

book_ref.quote: The underlying principle of the first law of thermodynamics is the conservation of energy.

blocks.prompt: 65 The first law of thermodynamics applies to:

options.text: all forms of energy and all types of processes

blocks.explanation: It applies universally, including chemical reactions, electrical systems and nuclear reactions (6.4).

book_ref.quote: applies universally to all forms of energy and all types of processes

blocks.prompt: 66 In an isolated system, according to the first law, the total energy:
blocks.explanation: Energy changes form but the total amount in an isolated system remains constant (6.4).

book_ref.quote: the total amount of energy in an isolated system remains constant over time

blocks.prompt: 67 A gas absorbs 250 J of heat and does 100 J of work on its surroundings. The change in its internal energy is:

book_ref.quote: In any thermodynamic process, when heat Q is added to a system

blocks.prompt: 68 A gas is compressed by doing 200 J of work on it, and at the same time it loses 50 J of heat. The change in its internal energy is:

book_ref.quote: Thus the change in internal energy ΔU = U₂ − U₁ is defined as Q − W.

blocks.prompt: 69 When a bicycle pump with a blocked outlet is pushed rapidly, the air inside becomes hot because:

options.text: work done on the air increases its internal energy
heat flows in from the hand
friction of the outlet cools it

blocks.explanation: The push force does work on the air, increasing its internal energy, shown by a rise in temperature (6.4).

book_ref.quote: When we pump on the handle rapidly, it becomes hot

blocks.prompt: 70 In the bicycle pump arrangement of Fig. 6.6, the air temperature is monitored by:

options.text: a thermocouple connected to a millivoltmeter

blocks.explanation: A thermocouple through the blocked outlet, read on a millivoltmeter, monitors the air temperature (Fig. 6.6).

book_ref.quote: A thermocouple connected through the blocked outlet allows the air temperature to be monitored.

blocks.prompt: 71 Energy transforming processes that occur within an organism are called:
blocks.explanation: Energy transforming processes within an organism are named metabolism (6.4).

book_ref.quote: Energy transforming processes that occur within an organism are named as metabolism.

blocks.prompt: 72 When a person does work, the decrease in internal energy of the body is made up by:
blocks.explanation: Work done decreases internal energy of the body; the internal energy is maintained by the food we eat (6.4).

book_ref.quote: the body temperature or in other words internal energy is maintained by the food we eat

blocks.prompt: 73 A process carried out at constant temperature is called:
blocks.explanation: An isothermal process is carried out at constant temperature (6.4).

book_ref.quote: It is a process which is carried out at constant temperature

blocks.prompt: 74 In an isothermal change of an ideal gas, the first law reduces to:
blocks.explanation: Internal energy depends only on temperature, which is constant, so ΔU = 0 and Q = W (6.4).

book_ref.quote: therefore, ΔU = 0. Hence, the first law of thermodynamics reduces to

blocks.prompt: 75 An ideal gas expands isothermally and absorbs 300 J of heat. The work done by the gas is:
blocks.explanation: Isothermal: ΔU = 0, so W = Q = 300 J (6.4).

book_ref.quote: an amount of heat Q has to be supplied to the gas in order to produce an isothermal change

blocks.prompt: 76 For an isothermal change, the expansion or compression must take place slowly because:
blocks.explanation: Since heat transfer takes time, the change must be slow to keep the temperature constant (6.4).

book_ref.quote: to keep the temperature of the gas constant, the expansion or compression must take place slowly

blocks.prompt: 77 The curve representing an isothermal process on a P-V diagram is called:

options.text: a straight line through the origin

blocks.explanation: The curve of an isothermal process is called an isotherm (Fig. 6.7-a).

book_ref.quote: The curve representing an isothermal process is called an isotherm

blocks.prompt: 78 A process in which no heat enters or leaves the system is called:
blocks.explanation: In an adiabatic process no heat enters or leaves the system, ΔQ = 0 (6.4).

book_ref.quote: An adiabatic process is the one in which no heat enters or leaves the system.

blocks.prompt: 79 In an adiabatic expansion, a gas does 80 J of external work. The change in its internal energy is:
blocks.explanation: Adiabatic: Q = 0, so W = −ΔU and ΔU = −80 J; the work is done at the expense of internal energy (6.4).

book_ref.quote: it is done at the expense of the internal energy of its molecules

blocks.prompt: 80 When a gas is compressed adiabatically, its temperature:
blocks.explanation: Adiabatic compression raises the temperature because work is done on the gas (6.4).

book_ref.quote: an adiabatic compression causes the temperature of the gas to rise

blocks.prompt: 81 Which one of the following is an example of an adiabatic process?

options.text: Rapid escape of air from a burst tyre
Slow melting of ice in a room
Slow compression of a gas in a cylinder kept in water

blocks.explanation: The rapid escape of air from a burst tyre is an adiabatic process (6.4).

book_ref.quote: The rapid escape of air from a burst tyre.

blocks.prompt: 82 Cloud formation in the atmosphere is an example of:
blocks.explanation: The chapter lists cloud formation among adiabatic processes (6.4).

book_ref.quote: Cloud formation in the atmosphere.

blocks.prompt: 83 For an adiabatic process PV^γ = constant, where γ is:

options.text: molar specific heat at constant volume / molar specific heat at constant pressure
molar specific heat at constant pressure / molar specific heat at constant volume
the ratio of final to initial temperature

blocks.explanation: γ is the ratio of the molar specific heat at constant pressure to that at constant volume (6.4).

book_ref.quote: where γ is the ratio of the molar specific heat of the gas at constant pressure

blocks.prompt: 84 Adiabatic change occurs most readily when the gas is:

options.text: expanded very slowly in a conducting cylinder
expanded or compressed rapidly in an insulated cylinder
kept in thermal contact with a large reservoir

blocks.explanation: Adiabatic change occurs when the gas expands or is compressed rapidly, particularly in an insulated cylinder (6.4).

book_ref.quote: Adiabatic change occurs when the gas expands or is compressed rapidly

blocks.prompt: 85 A process that can be retraced in exactly reverse order without producing any change in the surroundings is:
blocks.explanation: This is the definition of a reversible process (6.5).

book_ref.quote: A reversible process is one which can be retraced in exactly reverse order

blocks.prompt: 86 In a reversible process, if heat is absorbed in the direct process then in the reverse process heat is:
blocks.explanation: Thermal and mechanical effects at each stage are exactly reversed (6.5).

book_ref.quote: If heat is absorbed in the direct process, it will be given out in the reverse process

blocks.prompt: 87 A succession of events which brings a system back to its initial condition is called:
blocks.explanation: Such a succession of events is a cycle; a reversible cycle has all changes reversible (6.5).

book_ref.quote: A succession of events which brings the system back to its initial condition is called a cycle.

blocks.prompt: 88 Which of the following is practically reversible?
blocks.explanation: Liquefaction and evaporation performed slowly are practically reversible (6.5).

book_ref.quote: the processes of liquification and evaporation of a substance, performed slowly, are practically reversible

blocks.prompt: 89 An example of a highly irreversible process is:
blocks.explanation: Sudden changes and those involving friction or dissipation are irreversible; an explosion is highly irreversible (6.5).

book_ref.quote: An example of highly irreversible process is an explosion.

blocks.prompt: 90 Which type of change is always irreversible?

options.text: A very slow change in equilibrium
A change with all effects exactly reversed
A slow compression of a gas

blocks.explanation: Changes that occur suddenly or involve friction or dissipation of energy are irreversible (6.5).

book_ref.quote: All changes which occur suddenly or which involve friction

blocks.prompt: 91 A heat engine is a device that converts:

options.text: some thermal energy into mechanical work
all heat from one reservoir into work

blocks.explanation: A heat engine converts some thermal energy to mechanical work (6.6).

book_ref.quote: A heat engine converts some thermal energy to mechanical work.

blocks.prompt: 92 The earliest heat engine was the:
blocks.explanation: The earliest heat engine was the steam engine (6.6).

book_ref.quote: The earliest heat engine was the steam engine.

blocks.prompt: 93 The idea of the steam engine came from the observation that, when water boils in a covered vessel, the steam:

options.text: tries to push the lid off

blocks.explanation: The steam tries to push the lid off, showing its ability to do work (6.6).

book_ref.quote: the steam inside tries to push the lid off showing the ability to do work

blocks.prompt: 94 The working principle of a heat engine involves cyclic transfer of heat:

options.text: from a low temperature reservoir to a high temperature reservoir
from a high temperature reservoir to a low temperature reservoir
from the engine to the fuel

blocks.explanation: Heat is transferred cyclically from a high temperature reservoir to a low temperature reservoir, converting part of it into work (6.6).

book_ref.quote: the cyclic transfer of heat energy from a high temperature reservoir to a low temperature reservoir

blocks.prompt: 95 The first law says heat can be converted into an equivalent amount of work, but it is silent about:

options.text: the conditions under which this conversion takes place
the sign of work done by a gas

blocks.explanation: The second law deals with the circumstances of converting heat into work and the direction of heat flow (6.7).

book_ref.quote: but it is silent about the conditions under which this conversion takes place

blocks.prompt: 96 An engine absorbs 800 J from the hot reservoir and expels 600 J to the cold reservoir in each cycle. The work done per cycle is:
blocks.explanation: In a cycle ΔU = 0, so W = Q₁ − Q₂ = 800 − 600 = 200 J (6.7).

book_ref.quote: Hence, from the first law of thermodynamics, net work done should be equal to the net heat absorbed.

blocks.prompt: 97 For a working substance taken through a complete cycle, the change in internal energy is:
blocks.explanation: The substance returns to its initial state, so the change in internal energy is zero (6.7).

book_ref.quote: As the working substance goes through a cyclic process

blocks.prompt: 98 According to the chapter, a petrol engine converts roughly what fraction of the available heat energy into work?
blocks.explanation: Petrol engines convert roughly 25% and diesel engines 35 to 40% (6.7).

book_ref.quote: petrol engines convert roughly 25% and diesel engines 35 to 40% available heat energy into work
